summaries.gardner: Bank of America is a mature, regulated incumbent rather than a Rule Breaker: it does not lead an emerging industry, its shares have lagged the market (about 8% higher over five years to $51.41), and few commentators call it overvalued. Its well-known brand and digital lead (Erica, 50 million active digital users) are the closest fits to Gardner's traits.
summaries.buffett: Berkshire Hathaway has long been a major holder, drawn by its low-cost deposit franchise ($2.04 trillion of deposits) and Brian Moynihan's 'responsible growth' discipline. The fit is reasonable on understandability, consistent profits since 2011 and a modest price (about 13.5 times 2025 EPS and 1.3 times book), but returns (14.2% ROTCE in 2025) rely on leverage and Berkshire has been trimming its stake.
summaries.munger: Munger would see a durable, scale-based deposit franchise run by a sensible manager, but also a highly leveraged business where errors (2008's Countrywide purchase, the 2026 $1.2B anti-money-laundering penalty) can be costly. It is a fair business at a fair price rather than a great business at a fair price.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would class it as a stalwart or cyclical: a familiar name whose earnings follow interest rates and credit. At about 11.6 times 2026 consensus EPS with roughly 14% EPS growth expected in 2027 and a falling share count (diluted shares down from 8,797M in 2020 to 7,222M in Q3 2026), the PEG looks reasonable, but it is far from overlooked by Wall Street.
summaries.fisher: Fisher's emphasis on sales growth, research and outstanding people fits only partly: Bank of America has steady but modest revenue growth (about 6% a year from 2022 to 2025) and strong digital innovation, but it is not a product-development company and its margins depend heavily on interest rates.
summaries.graham: It passes several of Graham's defensive tests: a very large company, profitable every year since 2011, dividends paid every year for decades and EPS up from $1.31 in 2015 to $3.81 in 2025. At about 15.3 times three-year average EPS and P/E × P/B near 17.7 it is around the edge of his price limits, and it lacks the low-leverage balance sheet he preferred.
summaries.thiel: Bank of America fails most of Thiel's seven questions: it has no proprietary technology 10x better than rivals and competes in a crowded, mature market with JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and Citi. Its strengths are distribution and durability rather than a secret or monopoly.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders riding big platform shifts at sensible prices with management focused on efficiency. Bank of America is cheap and is using AI across 200,000+ employees, but its revenue growth of high single digits and exposure to rates make it a value cyclical rather than a secular-growth winner.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller trades liquidity and earnings momentum: higher rates and loan growth lifted net interest income 8% in Q3 2026 with about 8% growth guided for 2026 and 8%+ for 2027, but the Q3 miss, the $1.2B penalty and a 4.7% one-day fall break the near-term momentum. It would be a macro call on rates and the yield curve rather than a high-conviction position.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids banks because they rely on leverage and cannot earn high unleveraged returns on capital; Bank of America's 14.2% ROTCE is earned on a balance sheet more than ten times equity. It fails his 'good company' test even if the price is not demanding.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula's return on capital and earnings yield are not meaningful for banks, and Greenblatt excludes financials from the screen. On a simple earnings yield (about 7.4% at 13.5 times 2025 EPS) it looks moderately cheap.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a high-return business, skilled and honest managers and reinvestment opportunities. Bank of America has capable, long-tenured management but only moderate returns (14.2% ROTCE) and returns most of its earnings through dividends and buybacks rather than reinvesting at high rates.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai likes simple, durable businesses bought at deep discounts after a temporary setback. The October 2026 penalty and earnings miss are a fixable setback and the shares trade at about 1.3 times book, but the discount is modest rather than a Dhandho-style 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' bargain.
summaries.wood: Bank of America is an incumbent that ARK's research expects to be disrupted by digital wallets, stablecoins and decentralised finance. It does not lead any of ARK's innovation platforms, so it is a poor fit for Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: Ackman seeks simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and low leverage. Bank of America is large and dominant in US deposits and returns capital heavily ($8.2B in Q3 2026), but it is highly leveraged and its earnings depend on rates and credit, which Ackman's criteria avoid.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model needs a company that passes savings to customers and grows ever harder to compete with. Bank of America shares some scale benefits through Preferred Rewards and free digital tools, but its mature market position is unlikely to be clearly stronger in 10-20 years.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge markets with new technology. A 100-plus-year-old regulated bank is outside that model, though it does serve a very large market and solves a real need for safe deposits and credit.
summaries.nash: Bank of America fails most of Nash's screens: revenue growth is below 10%, debt exceeds cash, its five-year return badly trails the S&P 500, it faces a major regulatory issue (2026 OCC and FinCEN consent orders) and it is not built for a secular trend. Its scale, profitability and low forward P/E (about 11.6x) are the main positives.

momentum.evidence: The shares closed at $51.41 on October 14, 2026, about flat from $51.30 a year earlier and down from $61.95 in July 2026, lagging the S&P 500.

g4.evidence: CEO Brian Moynihan has led since 2010 and Berkshire Hathaway remains a major holder, though Berkshire cut its stake by about 30 million shares in Q2 2026.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly see it as cheap: 21 of 25 rate it Buy or Strong Buy with an average target of $66.59, about 30% above the price.

simple.evidence: Its business of taking deposits, lending and advising is familiar, but a $3.4 trillion balance sheet with trading, derivatives and rate sensitivity is hard for a generalist to analyse fully.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable every year since 2011, with net income between $17.9B (2020) and $32.0B (2021) and $30.5B in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management is candid and disciplined on capital, but Moynihan's pay rose to $41M for 2025 and the 2026 $1.2B anti-money-laundering penalty points to governance gaps; he also holds both chairman and CEO roles.

b6.evidence: Under Moynihan it has avoided large acquisitions since the crisis, sold 23 non-core businesses early in his tenure and grown organically under 'responsible growth'.

roic.evidence: Return on tangible common equity was a moderate 14.2% in 2025 and depends on leverage, with total liabilities of $3.13 trillion against $296.7B of equity in September 2026.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow is not a meaningful measure for a bank, whose operating cash flow swings with trading and balance-sheet movements; it instead returns capital, $8.2B in Q3 2026.

b10.evidence: Tangible book value per share rose to $29.14 in September 2026 from $28.73 at end-2025, but the share price is only about 8% above five years ago despite retained earnings.

safety.evidence: At about 1.3 times book value ($39.26) and 13.5 times 2025 EPS the price is modest, but it is not far below a conservative value for a bank earning 14% on tangible equity.

fairprice.evidence: At about 11.6 times 2026 consensus EPS of $4.44 with about 14% EPS growth expected in 2027 and a 2.5% dividend yield, the price is reasonable for its quality.

mu5.evidence: It is well capitalised (10.9% CET1 ratio) and backed by sticky deposits, but leverage means a deep credit crisis, deposit run or major compliance failure could badly hurt shareholders, as in 2008-2011.

reinvest.evidence: It returns most of its earnings through dividends and buybacks ($6.0B of repurchases in Q3 2026) because it cannot reinvest at high returns in a mature market.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear stalwart or rate-cyclical: a giant US bank whose story is net interest income growth (guided about 8% in 2026 and 8%+ in 2027) and buybacks.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 11.6 is below the roughly 14% EPS growth analysts expect for 2027 ($4.44 to $5.06).

runway.evidence: It is expanding into new US cities and growing wealth management ($5.1 trillion of client balances, up 9%), but overall revenue growth is about 6-9% a year and it is constrained by US deposit caps on acquisitions.

ly7.evidence: The company is shrinking its share count (period-end shares fell from 7,212M at end-2025 to 6,923M in September 2026), but insiders are not buying; the Chief Risk Officer sold 126,756 shares in 2026.

ly8.evidence: It is one of the most widely followed US stocks, covered by about 25 analysts and about 71% owned by institutions.

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching digital tools (Erica, CashPro, AI used by over 200,000 employees), but its core products are mature banking services.

fi3.evidence: Technology investment shows results, with 71% of consumer sales made digitally in Q3 2026 (up from 66%) and 3.6 billion digital interactions a quarter, though it does not report R&D.

fi4.evidence: It has added net checking accounts for 31 straight quarters and over 1 million new card accounts in Q3 2026, but it is not clearly better at selling than JPMorgan.

longterm.evidence: Moynihan's 'responsible growth' and steady technology investment favour the long term, but heavy buybacks and a focus on quarterly returns are typical of a mature bank.

gr1.evidence: It is the second-largest US bank, with $3.43 trillion of assets and a market value of about $356B.

ni10.evidence: It was profitable in each year from 2016 to 2025, with the low point $17.9B in 2020.

gr4.evidence: It has paid a common dividend every year for decades, including the token $0.01 quarterly dividend of 2009-2013, and paid $1.08 per share in 2025.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $1.31 in 2015 to $3.81 in 2025, almost tripling.

gr6.evidence: The price is about 15.3 times average diluted EPS for 2023-2025 ($3.05, $3.19, $3.81), right at Graham's limit.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 13.5 times P/B of about 1.31 gives roughly 17.7, below 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its technology, such as the Erica assistant, is good but not ten times better than JPMorgan's or other large banks' apps.

timing.evidence: Higher rates and repricing of its securities book are lifting net interest income (up 8% in Q3 2026), but falling rates would cut about $1.9B per 100bp drop.
